content: The Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions provides a detailed guide on how to prepare and maintain Cochrane systematic reviews that assess the effects of healthcare interventions. Members of the guideline development group were asked to indicate their positions on recommendations and provide judgments on the associated harms and benefits. They also evaluated the strength of the recommendations based on several factors: the desirable and undesirable effects of the intervention, the quality of the available evidence, the values and preferences related to the intervention in different settings, and the cost and feasibility of the intervention in various contexts. These aspects were openly discussed during meetings, and individual members documented their primary considerations on forms. Subsequent deliberations among the group members were conducted privately. The WHO Secretariat compiled and disclosed a summary of the results to the group. If unanimous consensus was not achieved, additional time was allocated for further deliberations, followed by a second round of online voting. If consensus was still not reached, a two-thirds majority vote was required to approve the proposed recommendations. Divergent opinions were allowed to be recorded in the guideline. Voting results were retained by WHO for up to five years. WHO staff and external technical experts involved in evidence collection and grading did not participate in the consensus-building process. Two co-chairs with expertise in group management and evidence interpretation were nominated and approved at the start of each consultation. WHO Secretariat members were present to guide the meeting process but did not vote or have veto power. Regarding the management of competing interests, all experts participating in WHO meetings were required to declare any relevant interests before their involvement. These declarations were reviewed by the responsible technical officer and relevant departments before finalizing the group composition and issuing invitations. Participants submitted a declaration-of-interest form and their curriculum vitae before each meeting, as mandated by the Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics, and WHO policy. Participants acted in their individual capacities, not as institutional representatives, and verbally declared potential conflicts of interest at the start of each meeting. The management of competing interests adhered strictly to WHO guidelines. For example, Dr. Hector Bourges Rodriguez declared his role as chair of the Board of Directors of the Danone Institute in Mexico, a non-profit organization funded by Danone Mexico. Since Danone does not manufacture products or make claims related to rice fortification, he was allowed to fully participate in the deliberations and decision-making process. Dr. Luz Maria De-Regil, who works for Nutrition International and co-authored a systematic review on rice fortification, participated in evidence deliberations but recused herself from decision-making on the recommendations. Similarly, Dr. Lynette Neufeld, employed by the Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition, participated in evidence discussions but recused herself from decision-making. Ms. Carol Tom, employed by USAID and a consultant for the East, Central, and Southern African Health Community, was deemed to have no conflict of interest and participated fully in the process. External experts also declared their interests but did not participate in deliberations or decision-making. The WHO Secretariat will continue to monitor research developments in rice fortification, particularly in areas with limited or low-quality evidence. If an update to the guideline is warranted, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development will coordinate the process following WHO’s formal procedures. As the guideline approaches its 10-year review period, a search for new evidence will be conducted to ensure its validity.
